newsitem.title: POLAND: FINANCE MINISTER VOWS MEASURES TO AVOID CZECH-STYLE SLUMP.
newsitem.headline: FINANCE MINISTER VOWS MEASURES TO AVOID CZECH-STYLE SLUMP.

text.p: Finance Minister Marek Belka on Wednesday vowed that Poland will tighten its fiscal policy and keep austere monetary measures to avoid an economic performance slump, which hit its southern neighbour, the Czech Republic.

"We are looking with concern at the situation developing in the Czech Republic.... We must act to make sure that the situation (in the Czech Republic) is not repeated in Poland," Belka told a news conference.

He said the finance ministry would propose cutting the budget deficit next year and that the central bank would maintain its high real interest rates policy to ensure that a foreign trade gap does not undermine economic growth.

"It is not enough to keep the monetary policy tight, the budgetary policy must also be tightened. Hence, it is a duty of the finance ministry to construct such a (1998) budget in which a smaller deficit was possible," he said.

On Tuesday, the central bank's head Hanna Gronkiewicz-Waltz said the 1998 budget draft would provide for cutting the deficit to 1.8 percent of gross domestic product from this year's planned 2.8 percent.
"I do not know whether the budget deficit will be as tight as the central bank president said but we are certainly going in that direction," Belka said.
He added it would be hard to finance next year's deficit at the 1997 level anyway, because it had already been difficult to place some treasuries on the market.

Belka said the planned deficit cut and the high real official rates policy should help Poland, where the economy is firmly expanding and inflation falling, to avoid difficulties experienced by the Czech Republic.

The Czech Republic faces macroeconomic problems, mainly a current account deficit of more than nine percent of gross domestic product and falling industrial output, which have cut the value of the Czech crown on foreign exchange markets.
The slump followed several years of demand-led growth as industry imported technology and a sharp rise in wages provoked a consumer boom.
The Czech economic hurdles prompted political instability and the three parties in the ruling Czech coalition agreed on Wednesday to make changes in the makeup of the cabinet.

Poland has also experienced a consumer boom, fuelled by rapid credit expansion, which allowed economic growth to slow down only to six percent last year from seven percent in 1995 despite a much slower pace of exports increase.

Polish current account gap is expected to rise to 3-3.5 percent of GDP this year from one percent in 1996, which officials have said was not yet worrying but that measures had to be taken now, before it is too late.

The central bank, concerned that the economy may be overheating, raised banks' obligatory reserves on call deposits and then on term deposits from 17 and nine percent to 20 and 11 perecent respectively, in a move to curb credit action.
But Belka said that Poland's falling inflation, which dropped to 15.3 percent in April from 18.5 percent in December last year, made him optimistic, provided the monetary policy remained thight.
He said he was confident that year-on-year inflation would fall to 13 percent or less in December.
"The economy is in high gear and I am sometimes concerned that it may be too high, but falling inflation soothes my fears," he said.
